paragraphs: The paper asks how people judge causal relationships when causes vary continuously. Earlier rational models had explained judgments mainly using binary observations, such as whether a cause and an outcome were present or absent. That setup leaves out information whenever observations differ by degree rather than falling into two categories.

The authors develop a rational model that works with continuous dimensions. Its purpose is to bring formal accounts of causal reasoning closer to the kinds of evidence people encounter outside simplified binary tasks. The central change is therefore in the information the model can accommodate, while retaining the goal of explaining human causal judgments.

The model predicts judgments from previous studies better than models designed for discrete causal inference. In a new experiment, it also explains participants’ inferences better than several plausible alternatives that accommodate continuous causes. These comparisons support the proposed account in the studies examined and show why explicitly representing continuous variation can matter when modeling human causal reasoning.
neurips-2011-a-rational-model-of-causal-.tldr: A rational model using continuous causes explains human causal judgments better than the compared discrete and continuous alternatives in the reported studies.

paragraphs: An object’s perceived identity can depend on the orientation against which it is interpreted. A cross, for example, can be read differently after rotation. Real scenes can contain several such reference frames, so understanding an ambiguous image requires deciding which surrounding orientation provides the appropriate context.

The authors propose an ideal observer model using nonparametric Bayesian statistics. It infers both how many reference frames a scene contains and the parameters describing them. This lets the model address scenes with multiple competing frames rather than assuming that every image belongs to a single shared frame.

For an image compatible with two conflicting frames, the model predicts two influences. Proximity favors the frame associated with a nearby object, while alignment favors the frame containing more objects. Using a new method for testing human reference frame inference, the authors confirm that people use both cues. The findings support these specific predictions about how spatial context guides interpretation when an image is ambiguous.
neurips-2011-an-ideal-observer-model-for.tldr: An ideal observer model predicts, and behavioral tests confirm, that proximity and alignment influence how people assign ambiguous images to reference frames.

paragraphs: Researchers sometimes want to model individual behavior even though their observations contain only totals or small tables of counts. In this setting, the available evidence summarizes a population rather than recording each person separately. The paper develops a framework for carrying out probabilistic modeling and inference directly from this aggregate information.

Collective Graphical Models operate on the sufficient statistics of an individual-level model. These are the summaries that retain the information needed for inference within that model. Making these summaries the objects of inference provides a way to connect a model of individuals with observations that are available only collectively.

The authors derive an efficient Gibbs sampling algorithm for the posterior distribution of these statistics, conditioned on noisy aggregate observations. This means the method represents uncertainty about the underlying summaries while accounting for noise in the observed counts. They prove the sampler’s correctness and demonstrate its effectiveness experimentally. The contribution combines a modeling framework suited to aggregate data with a computational procedure for performing its inference.
neurips-2011-collective-graphical-models.tldr: Collective Graphical Models enable inference about individual-level models through sufficient statistics observed only as noisy aggregates.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to release statistical estimates while providing differential privacy. Its focus is a broad family of procedures called M-estimators. A central challenge is to preserve useful statistical information without requiring the data-release process to know in advance exactly which inference procedure will later be used.

The proposed approach uses perturbed histograms as the basis for releasing estimates. By working through this shared representation, the method supports a wide class of M-estimators while combining a privacy guarantee with statistical utility. The ability to avoid choosing the particular inference procedure beforehand is a defining feature of the approach.

The authors analyze convergence rates to characterize the method’s statistical performance as the amount of data grows. They also provide a practical algorithm and apply it to a real dataset containing both continuous and categorical variables. Together, the analysis and application connect the general release strategy to an implementable procedure, showing how privacy-preserving estimation can accommodate mixed kinds of data.
neurips-2011-differentially-private-m-es.tldr: Perturbed histograms support differentially private release of a wide class of M-estimators without choosing the inference procedure in advance.

paragraphs: A neuron’s voltage trace is observable, but the input signals and ion channel states underlying it are partly hidden. This paper develops a Bayesian method for estimating those changing quantities from a single trace. The targets include both the mean and variance of synaptic input and the dynamics of each ion channel.

The method formulates the task as inference in a state-space model, linking observed voltage to hidden quantities that evolve over time. Prior distributions penalize large fluctuations in the parameters. This assumption favors smoother changes while allowing the estimates to vary, providing structure for interpreting a single measured signal.

The authors choose hyperparameters by maximizing marginal likelihood, then use the fitted model to estimate input parameters and channel states over time. They test the method on simulated data from Hodgkin–Huxley type models and on experimental recordings from a cortical slice in vitro. The work thus brings several hidden aspects of neuronal dynamics into one inference procedure and examines it with both simulated and experimental voltage data.
neurips-2011-estimating-time-varying-inp.tldr: A Bayesian state-space method estimates changing synaptic input statistics and ion channel states from a single neuronal voltage trace.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequences of events occurring along a time axis. In an ordinary renewal process, intervals between events are independent draws from the same distribution. Modulated renewal processes allow that distribution to change with time, making them suitable for describing event patterns whose statistical behavior is not stationary.

The authors take a nonparametric Bayesian approach, using a Gaussian process to model the time variation. This places the changing behavior within a probabilistic framework rather than requiring a fixed, finite description of its temporal shape. The resulting model combines renewal-process interval structure with a flexible account of nonstationarity.

Computation is a central contribution. The approach uses uniformization to obtain exact samples from a distribution that would otherwise be intractable, and the authors develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler for posterior inference. They test their methods on synthetic and real datasets. The work therefore addresses both how to represent changing event statistics and how to perform inference in the resulting model.
neurips-2011-gaussian-process-modulated-.tldr: Gaussian processes model time variation in renewal processes, with uniformization supporting exact sampling and an efficient posterior inference algorithm.

paragraphs: High-dimensional learning becomes more manageable when a model has fewer effective degrees of freedom than its number of variables suggests. Sparsity, group sparsity, and low rank are examples of such structure. The paper seeks a common computational framework that can capture established approaches and support forms of structure beyond those already studied.

The authors propose and analyze a general greedy scheme for convex optimization problems arising from structural constraints. A greedy strategy builds a solution through successive choices. Here, the framework is broad enough to recover existing greedy algorithms as special cases and also produce new algorithms, linking methods that might otherwise require separate treatments.

The analysis also extends to infinite-dimensional problems. This extension uses connections between the smoothness of norms and the behavior of martingales in Banach spaces. The contribution is therefore both computational and theoretical: it supplies a shared algorithmic approach and develops mathematical tools for understanding its behavior across a wider range of structured problems.
neurips-2011-greedy-algorithms-for-struc.tldr: A general greedy optimization framework unifies existing algorithms for structured high-dimensional problems, yields new ones, and extends to infinite dimensions.

paragraphs: Hierarchical matching pursuit builds image representations one layer at a time. Its architecture combines an efficient matching pursuit encoder, spatial pyramid max pooling, and contrast normalization. The authors investigate these components and find that all three are important for good performance, making the overall representation more than a choice of encoding algorithm.

To accelerate encoding, they introduce batch tree orthogonal matching pursuit. It is particularly suited to processing many observations that share a large dictionary. This computational improvement helps HMP handle full-size images efficiently. The resulting features also allow linear support vector machines to match nonlinear support vector machine performance while remaining scalable to large datasets.

The experiments compare HMP with several established feature-learning approaches, including convolutional deep belief networks, SIFT-based sparse coding, and kernel-based methods. HMP achieves higher accuracy across the reported object, scene, and static-event recognition tasks. These results connect the architecture’s representation quality with its computational design: the hierarchy supports strong classification performance while the encoder makes processing larger collections practical.
neurips-2011-hierarchical-matching-pursu.tldr: Hierarchical matching pursuit combines layered image features with fast encoding to achieve superior reported classification accuracy and scalable linear classification.

paragraphs: Maximum entropy models can be used to estimate entropy and, in turn, mutual information in biological systems. When fitted to small datasets, however, their entropy estimates can be biased downward. This paper examines that sampling bias and asks how it depends on whether the chosen model class can represent the true data distribution.

When the data-generating distribution belongs to the model class, the authors show that the bias equals the number of parameters divided by twice the number of observations. This gives a direct relationship between model size, sample size, and bias under the stated modeling condition. The condition is essential to interpreting that expression.

The paper then studies misspecification, where the true distribution falls outside the model class, and shows that bias can be much larger. It provides a perturbative approximation to the maximally expected bias in that setting and illustrates the analysis with Ising-model simulations. The findings show why a bias calculation based only on parameter and observation counts may be inadequate when the model cannot represent the underlying distribution.
neurips-2011-how-biased-are-maximum-entr.tldr: Entropy estimates from maximum entropy models can have substantially greater sampling bias when the true distribution lies outside the model class.

paragraphs: The paper examines how people teach a robot a concept defined by a simple one-dimensional threshold. This task creates a useful comparison between two computational accounts of teaching: the teaching dimension model and the curriculum learning principle. In this setting, they make conflicting predictions about which teaching strategy should be optimal.

Behavioral studies reveal three distinct strategies used by human teachers. One is consistent with curriculum learning. Rather than treating all observed behavior as a single pattern, the authors develop a theoretical framework as a possible explanation for that particular strategy, connecting the teaching choices to an explicit objective for the learner.

The framework assumes that the teacher aims to minimize the learner’s expected generalization error at every iteration. It extends the standard teaching dimension model by incorporating concern for how well the learner performs during the teaching process. Under that objective, the framework offers a theoretical justification for curriculum learning. The result provides a potential account of one observed human strategy, without claiming that it explains all three.
neurips-2011-how-do-humans-teach-on-curr.tldr: Human teaching experiments reveal three strategies, and a model minimizing expected error at each step offers a potential explanation for the curriculum-like strategy.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the identification of brain regions associated with early Alzheimer’s disease. Signals from these regions may be weak in any single imaging modality. Because different modalities provide complementary measurements of disease pathology, analyzing them together may improve the ability to detect regions that would be difficult to identify separately.

The proposed sparse composite linear discriminant analysis model splits each discriminant parameter into two multiplied parts: one shared across modalities and one specific to a modality. This structure lets modalities contribute jointly while retaining their differences. The authors prove an equivalent formulation using a non-convex penalty and solve it through difference-of-convex programming, which also reveals the penalty’s ability to preserve weak-effect features.

Simulations show better feature selection than the compared algorithms, particularly for weak-effect features. The authors also analyze MRI and PET images from 49 patients with Alzheimer’s disease and 67 normal controls. The identified brain regions agree with findings in the Alzheimer’s literature. These results support the model’s use for identifying disease-related regions through combined imaging evidence.
neurips-2011-identifying-alzheimer-s-dis.tldr: A sparse model combining imaging modalities improves weak-feature selection in simulations and identifies Alzheimer’s-related brain regions consistent with prior findings.

paragraphs: The paper develops a generative model that interprets a road scene and its objects together in three dimensions. From a short video recorded by one camera on a moving car, it infers scene topology and geometry, object positions and orientations, and traffic activities. These quantities are handled within a joint model.

The model combines evidence that changes over time with evidence about the scene’s appearance and geometry. Short vehicle tracks provide dynamic information, while semantic labels and vanishing points provide static information. Bringing these cues together allows the inference process to use both observed motion and the spatial organization visible in the images.

In experiments, the approach outperforms a discriminative baseline based on multiple kernel learning that receives the same image information. The authors also report a significant improvement in the orientation estimates of state-of-the-art object detectors through their three-dimensional reasoning. The findings support the value of joint scene and object interpretation, with the equal-information comparison highlighting the contribution of the modeling approach.
neurips-2011-joint-3d-estimation-of-obje.tldr: Joint generative reasoning about road scenes and objects in 3D improves the reported scene interpretation and object-orientation results.

paragraphs: Estimating a person’s three-dimensional pose from images is ambiguous, so tracking systems often use learned pose priors to guide their estimates. The paper targets a difficulty in learning these priors: existing approaches can be overly simple, difficult to train, or restricted to latent representations of a single activity such as walking.

The authors introduce an efficient stochastic gradient descent algorithm for learning probabilistic nonlinear latent spaces containing multiple activities. Such a space provides a learned representation of pose variation that can accommodate more than one kind of movement. The contribution addresses both the flexibility of the representation and the computational problem of fitting it.

They also derive an incremental algorithm that updates the latent space in an online setting without extensive relearning. This extends the approach beyond a representation that must remain fixed after initial training. Experiments on monocular and multiple-view tracking demonstrate the method’s effectiveness and report performance above the state of the art. The results support using these richer learned pose representations for the tracking tasks examined.
neurips-2011-learning-probabilistic-non-.tldr: Efficient training and incremental updates make probabilistic nonlinear pose representations spanning multiple activities useful for improved human tracking.

paragraphs: Newtron addresses online prediction among multiple classes when feedback is limited to the bandit setting. The analysis allows a fully adversarial sequence rather than assuming a favorable data-generating process. The authors evaluate regret using a particular log-loss family controlled by a scalar parameter, alpha, so the guarantees depend on how that parameter is chosen.

The algorithm uses a new application of the online Newton method. For a constant alpha that does not change with the prediction horizon T, the authors prove regret of O(log T). When alpha may increase toward infinity with T, they establish an upper bound of O(T^(2/3)). These statements describe different parameter regimes.

For alpha of order O(log T), the regret bound is O(sqrt(T)), resolving the open problem identified in the paper. Experimental tests also show good performance even with a small constant alpha. The contribution combines an efficient algorithm with explicit theoretical guarantees under limited feedback, while making clear that the rate depends on the parameterized loss used for comparison.
neurips-2011-newtron-an-efficient-bandit.tldr: Newtron efficiently handles adversarial multiclass prediction with bandit feedback and provides regret bounds that depend on its log-loss parameter.

paragraphs: Image segmentation often starts from a flat collection of pixels or superpixels and assigns labels to those elements. The pylon model instead represents an image as a hierarchy of candidate segments. This makes it possible for the final partition to use regions from different levels of detail in different parts of the image.

The authors show that an energy combining unary and boundary terms on this hierarchical representation can still be optimized by graph cuts, retaining the associated efficiency and global optimality benefits for that formulation. The hierarchy therefore expands the available segmentation choices while preserving a useful optimization structure. Inference selects which segments from the tree form the resulting partition.

The model is applied to semantic segmentation, where regions correspond to semantic classes. Experiments demonstrate the advantage of reasoning over a segmentation tree and show that the method can flexibly choose segmentation levels across an image. The reported system achieves higher segmentation accuracy than previous approaches on Graz-02 and Stanford background, supporting the usefulness of this adaptive regional representation.
neurips-2011-pylon-model-for-semantic-se.tldr: The pylon model uses graph cuts on a segmentation hierarchy to select region detail flexibly and improve reported semantic segmentation accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate the spread of information when only some copies become public. It represents the full spread as an unobserved tree, with nodes randomly revealing their copies. For chain-letter petitions, the names recorded on a public copy disclose a path back to the tree’s root, exposing part of its history.

These revealed paths form an observed tree, but that tree is only a partial view of the underlying spread. The authors ask both what structural properties this visible portion has and whether it contains enough information to estimate the size of the full tree. Their analysis explicitly connects the observation mechanism to the structure researchers can see.

The paper provides the first algorithm for this size-estimation task, together with provable performance guarantees. It also establishes properties of the observed tree that give a rigorous explanation for some unusual structures found in real online chain-letter petitions. The contribution shows how incomplete public traces can support inference about a larger diffusion process under the stated tree-based observation model.
neurips-2011-reconstructing-patterns-of-.tldr: An algorithm with provable guarantees estimates the size of a hidden information-diffusion tree from randomly revealed paths.

paragraphs: The paper presents an algorithm for exactly solving decision problems expressed as influence diagrams. These representations describe decisions alongside the information relevant to making them. The focus is on limited-information problems, where the information available for a decision need not satisfy the assumptions commonly imposed by existing solution methods.

In particular, the algorithm does not require the usual no-forgetting and regularity assumptions. Removing those requirements broadens the range of decision problems it can address. Its computational core is a sophisticated variable elimination procedure, which organizes the solution through elimination of variables in the representation rather than treating the strategy space as an undifferentiated collection.

The authors evaluate the algorithm on randomly generated problems with up to 150 variables and 10^64 possible strategies. In those experiments, it outperforms a state-of-the-art algorithm. This result demonstrates an empirical computational advantage on the tested problems, while the exactness of the method is a separate contribution: it solves the represented decision problem exactly despite allowing the specified forms of limited information.
neurips-2011-solving-decision-problems-w.tldr: An exact variable-elimination algorithm solves influence-diagram decision problems without the usual no-forgetting and regularity assumptions.

paragraphs: Sparse estimation seeks a representation using relatively few dictionary components. Much theoretical work evaluates it with idealized dictionaries whose columns are normalized and weakly correlated. This paper instead considers structured dictionaries that may contain strongly correlated groups of columns or rows, bringing the analysis closer to settings where those ideal conditions fail.

The authors analyze sparsity-penalized regression to identify regimes where performance is invariant to dictionary structure, as far as possible. Their central example is a Type II Bayesian estimator whose sparsity penalty depends on the dictionary itself. That dependence lets the penalty account for structural properties that a conventional fixed penalty may not capture.

The estimator has several provable invariance properties that yield advantages over penalties such as the l1 norm, especially where existing recovery guarantees no longer apply. The authors explain that these advantages can translate into better performance for correlated-feature selection, source localization, and compressive sensing with constrained measurement directions. The claim is about particular advantageous regimes and potential application benefits, rather than unrestricted independence from the dictionary.
neurips-2011-sparse-estimation-with-stru.tldr: A dictionary-dependent Bayesian sparsity penalty offers provable invariance advantages in structured settings where conventional recovery guarantees may fail.

paragraphs: Sparse Manifold Clustering and Embedding addresses data lying on several nonlinear manifolds: separate low-dimensional structures embedded in a larger space. It aims to identify those groups and reduce their dimensionality together. Like many embedding methods, it builds weighted connections between each point and a small set of neighbors.

Its distinctive step is to choose both the neighbors and their weights automatically through sparse optimization. The objective encourages nearby points from the same manifold that approximately span a low-dimensional affine subspace. The resulting connections contain information used by spectral clustering and embedding, linking local geometric choices to the final grouping and representation.

Neighborhood sizes may differ from point to point, and the size selected for a point provides an estimate of its manifold’s dimension. Experiments show effective handling of nearby manifolds, uneven sampling, and holes, along with estimation of intrinsic dimensions. These findings support the usefulness of adapting neighborhoods to local structure when one fixed neighborhood choice would not reflect the varying geometry of the data.
neurips-2011-sparse-manifold-clustering-.tldr: SMCE automatically selects sparse neighborhoods to cluster multiple manifolds, embed their data, and estimate local intrinsic dimensions.

paragraphs: Sparse coding represents observations using a small selection of dictionary elements, called atoms. This paper adds structure by assigning penalties or interactions to pairs of atoms. With a dictionary of K atoms, these pairwise relationships provide a way to express how the choice of one element relates to the use of another.

The authors modify standard sparse coding algorithms to perform inference with these interactions included. Their experiments show that the resulting algorithms are efficient. This matters because adding relationships between dictionary elements changes the coding problem: inference must account for the structured interactions as well as choose a sparse representation of an observation.

The framework also supports dictionary learning. The authors demonstrate learned dictionaries with interactions expressing tree structures or local connectivity, showing that different relationship patterns can be incorporated into the same approach. Finally, the interaction values themselves can be learned from data instead of being fixed beforehand. This makes structure a learnable part of the representation alongside the dictionary, rather than solely a specification supplied in advance.
neurips-2011-structured-sparse-coding-vi.tldr: Pairwise interactions between dictionary atoms enable efficient structured sparse coding and allow the interaction strengths themselves to be learned.

paragraphs: The paper develops a classifier for examples that can have several labels at once, with a learning objective that attempts to optimize the F-score directly. Its model includes pairwise interactions favoring labels that occur together. These assortative interactions let predictions incorporate label co-occurrence instead of treating every label as an unrelated decision.

For a fitted model, prediction reduces to minimizing a submodular set function, which can be solved exactly and efficiently using graph cuts. Training presents a different computational challenge: it requires an intractable combinatorial optimization. The authors therefore introduce an approximate algorithm for that learning problem, separating tractable prediction from the harder process of fitting the model.

They prove a soundness property for the approximate procedure, described as never predicting incorrect labels, and provide a test of a sufficient condition for having reached an optimal solution. That optimality test is conditional, rather than a guarantee that every run finds the optimum. Benchmark experiments support the technique’s value, and the authors supply source code for reproducing their experiments.
neurips-2011-submodular-multi-label-lear.tldr: A multi-label model uses label co-occurrence for exact graph-cut prediction, with approximate training and a sufficient-condition test for optimality.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification depends on which examples are closest under the chosen distance metric. Learning feature weights changes that metric and can abruptly change the identities of the nearest neighbors. The paper addresses this target-neighbor change, which creates a consistency problem when an optimization method continues using neighbors selected under an earlier metric.

The authors propose a feature-weighting algorithm based on sequential quadratic programming that tracks the correct target neighbors exactly and efficiently. This keeps the neighbor choices consistent with the feature-space metric as learning proceeds. They describe it, to their knowledge, as the first algorithm to guarantee this consistency, addressing a difficulty they identify in previous feature-weighting and metric-learning work.

The method also combines naturally with regularization path tracking. Following how solutions change with regularization allows computationally efficient selection of the regularization parameter. Experiments demonstrate the algorithm’s effectiveness. The contribution thus connects two practical aspects of learning a distance metric: maintaining valid neighbor relationships during optimization and efficiently choosing the amount of regularization.
neurips-2011-target-neighbor-consistent-.tldr: A sequential quadratic programming method keeps target neighbors exactly consistent with learned feature weights and supports efficient regularization selection.

paragraphs: Temporal difference methods can combine return estimates spanning different numbers of steps. The authors show that the lambda-return used in TD(lambda) is a maximum likelihood estimator under a particular model of how return variance grows with the number of steps. This gives its weighting scheme a specific statistical interpretation.

They introduce a gamma-return based on a more accurate variance model and derive the TD gamma algorithm. It removes the lambda parameter, but updates only when an episode ends and requires time and memory proportional to episode length. A second version, TD gamma(C), introduces a capacity parameter C to enable incremental, online updates, using C times the time and memory of TD(lambda).

Across five benchmark domains, TD gamma outperforms TD(lambda) at every lambda setting on four domains. At intermediate capacity settings, TD gamma(C) performs as well as or better than TD gamma. These findings support revisiting how returns are combined, while the two algorithms expose different computational requirements for episodic and online use.
neurips-2011-td-gamma-re-evaluating-comp.tldr: A revised variance model yields TD gamma return estimators with strong reported benchmark performance and distinct episodic and online computation tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Off-policy learning evaluates a policy using experience generated while following another policy. For temporal difference learning with function approximation, convergence alone does not establish that the resulting value estimate is good. The paper shows that arbitrary off-policy sampling can produce unboundedly large error even when the approximation system can represent the true value function well.

The authors address this problem by identifying a particular convex subset of off-policy sampling distributions. Within this set, they can guarantee solution quality in a way similar to the on-policy case. The restriction on sampling distributions is therefore central: the guarantee does not extend to arbitrary off-policy sampling.

They also show how to project efficiently onto this convex set using only samples generated by the system. This makes the theoretical restriction part of a usable procedure, leading to a new temporal difference algorithm with approximation guarantees under off-policy sampling. Experiments show it outperforming existing temporal difference methods. The contribution links a condition ensuring solution quality to a practical way of enforcing that condition.
neurips-2011-the-fixed-points-of-off-pol.tldr: Restricting off-policy sampling to a suitable convex set yields temporal difference approximation guarantees and a practical sample-based algorithm.

paragraphs: Transfer reinforcement learning uses experience from previously encountered tasks to help solve a target task. This paper studies a direct form of transfer: taking samples collected on source tasks and adding them to the training data for the target. The approach makes previously gathered experience available to the target learning algorithm.

The authors investigate the theoretical properties of this sample-transfer method and introduce algorithms that adapt the transfer process according to source–target similarity. This puts task relatedness at the center of the transfer decision. With several possible sources, the method considers their relationship to the target when determining how to use their experience.

The paper also presents illustrative experiments on a continuous chain problem. These experiments accompany the theoretical investigation and the proposed adaptive algorithms. The main contribution is a principled treatment of a simple reuse mechanism: transferring samples becomes a process guided by similarity between tasks, connecting the general goal of faster reinforcement learning to decisions about which source experience should inform the target.
neurips-2011-transfer-from-multiple-mdps.tldr: The paper analyzes sample transfer between reinforcement-learning tasks and proposes algorithms that adapt transfer to source–target similarity.
